subject: Computer Science
summary: Covers security goals and attacks, malware types, symmetric and public-key cryptography (DES, AES, RSA, Diffie–Hellman), hashing, digital signatures and certificates, firewalls, authentication and secure protocols, and Indian cyber law under the IT Act, 2000 with its 2008 amendment. DSSSB questions test definitions (worm vs virus vs Trojan, firewall types, SSL, digital certificates) and the main IT Act sections and penalties.

sections.heading: Security goals, services and attack types
sections.body:
The core goals form the **CIA triad**:
- **Confidentiality**: only authorised people can read data (achieved by encryption, access control).
- **Integrity**: data is not altered without detection (hashes, MACs, digital signatures).
- **Availability**: systems and data are accessible when needed (backups, redundancy, DoS protection).
Further services (ITU-T X.800): **authentication** (proving identity), **access control**, and **non-repudiation** (a sender cannot later deny sending; provided by digital signatures).
A **vulnerability** is a weakness, a **threat** is a possible danger that may exploit it, an **attack** is the actual attempt, and **risk** = likelihood × impact.
**Passive attacks** only observe: release of message contents (eavesdropping) and **traffic analysis**. They are hard to detect, so the defence is prevention (encryption).
**Active attacks** change or disrupt: **masquerade** (pretending to be someone else), **replay** (re-sending captured messages), **modification of messages** and **denial of service**. The defence is detection and recovery.
**Hackers** may be white-hat (ethical, authorised testing), black-hat (malicious, also called crackers) or grey-hat.

sections.heading: Malware: viruses, worms, Trojans and more
sections.body:
**Malware** (malicious software) is any program written to harm, steal or gain unauthorised control.
- A **virus** attaches itself to a host file or program and spreads when that host is run or shared; it needs user action.
- A **worm** is a standalone program that **self-replicates across a network without user action**, often eating bandwidth (the Morris worm of 1988 was an early example).
- A **Trojan horse** looks useful but performs hidden harmful actions; it does **not** replicate.
**Virus types**: boot-sector (infects the boot record; Brain, 1986, is regarded as the first IBM-PC virus), file infector, **macro virus** (inside documents such as Word/Excel files), **polymorphic** (changes its code each time to evade signatures), **metamorphic**, **stealth** (hides changes it makes), **multipartite** (boot sector + files) and memory-resident.
**Protection**: updated antivirus (signature and heuristic scanning), OS patches, not opening unknown attachments, backups, least privilege.

sections.heading: Network attacks and social engineering
sections.body:
- **Phishing**: fake e-mails or websites that trick users into revealing passwords or card details. Variants: **spear phishing** (targeted at a person), **whaling** (targets senior executives), **vishing** (voice calls), **smishing** (SMS).
- **Pharming**: redirects users from a genuine site to a fake one by poisoning DNS or the hosts file.
- **Spoofing**: forging the source identity (IP spoofing, e-mail spoofing, ARP spoofing, caller-ID spoofing).
- **Sniffing / eavesdropping**: capturing traffic on a network.
- **Man-in-the-middle (MITM)**: the attacker secretly relays and possibly alters messages between two parties.
- **DoS / DDoS**: flooding a server so genuine users cannot get service (SYN flood, ping flood); DDoS uses many machines (a botnet).
- **SQL injection**: malicious SQL inserted through input fields; **cross-site scripting (XSS)**: malicious script injected into web pages.
- **Password attacks**: brute force (try all combinations), dictionary attack, credential stuffing.
- **Zero-day attack**: exploits a flaw before a patch exists.
- **Salami attack**: many tiny thefts (e.g. paise from many accounts); **data diddling**: altering data before or during entry.
- **Social engineering**: manipulating people — pretexting, baiting, **shoulder surfing**, **dumpster diving**, **tailgating**.
- **Cyberstalking**, **cyberbullying**, **identity theft** and **email bombing** are common cyber crimes against individuals.

sections.heading: Cryptography basics and classical ciphers
sections.body:
**Cryptography** converts readable **plaintext** into unreadable **ciphertext** (**encryption**) and back (**decryption**) using an algorithm (cipher) and a **key**. **Cryptanalysis** is breaking ciphers; cryptography + cryptanalysis = **cryptology**. **Kerckhoffs's principle**: the algorithm may be public; security must depend only on the secrecy of the key.
**Classical techniques:**
- **Substitution cipher**: each letter is replaced by another. **Caesar cipher** shifts each letter by a fixed amount (Caesar used 3); only 25 useful keys, so brute force is trivial. Monoalphabetic substitution falls to **frequency analysis**; polyalphabetic ciphers such as **Vigenère** use several shifts.
- **Transposition cipher**: letters are rearranged, not replaced (rail fence, columnar transposition).
- **One-time pad**: random key as long as the message, used once; theoretically unbreakable.
**Steganography** hides the very existence of a message (e.g. inside an image), while cryptography hides its meaning.
Modern ciphers are **block ciphers** (fixed-size blocks, e.g. AES) or **stream ciphers** (bit/byte at a time, e.g. RC4).

sections.heading: Symmetric-key cryptography
sections.body:
In **symmetric (secret/private-key) cryptography** the **same key** encrypts and decrypts. It is fast and used for bulk data, but the key must be shared secretly (**key distribution problem**), and n users need n(n − 1)/2 keys for every pair to communicate privately.
- **DES**: 64-bit block, **56-bit effective key** (64 bits with 8 parity bits), 16 rounds, Feistel structure; now insecure because 2⁵⁶ keys can be searched.
- **3DES (Triple DES)**: applies DES three times (encrypt–decrypt–encrypt) with two or three keys (112 or 168 key bits).
- **AES** (Rijndael): **128-bit block**, keys of **128, 192 or 256 bits** with **10, 12 or 14 rounds**; a substitution–permutation network, not Feistel; the current standard.
- **IDEA**: 64-bit block, 128-bit key. **Blowfish**: 64-bit block, variable key up to 448 bits. **RC4**: stream cipher (now considered weak).
**Modes of operation** for block ciphers: ECB (identical blocks give identical ciphertext — insecure for patterns), CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR.

sections.heading: Public-key cryptography: RSA and Diffie–Hellman
sections.body:
In **asymmetric (public-key) cryptography** each user has a **key pair**: a **public key** (shared openly) and a **private key** (kept secret). What one key encrypts, only the other can decrypt. n users need only n key pairs (2n keys).
- **Confidentiality**: encrypt with the **receiver's public key**; only the receiver's private key decrypts.
- **Authentication / digital signature**: encrypt (sign) with the **sender's private key**; anyone verifies with the sender's public key.
**RSA** (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, 1977) relies on the difficulty of **factoring** a large n = p × q:
- Choose primes p, q; n = p × q; φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1).
- Choose e with 1 < e < φ(n) and gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1; find d with e·d ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)).
- Public key (e, n); private key (d, n). Encrypt C = Mᵉ mod n; decrypt M = Cᵈ mod n.
**Diffie–Hellman** (1976) lets two parties agree on a shared secret over an open channel; it relies on the **discrete logarithm** problem. It provides key exchange only (no encryption or signature) and, without authentication, is open to man-in-the-middle attacks.
**ECC** (elliptic-curve cryptography) gives equal security with much shorter keys. Practical systems are **hybrid**: public-key exchange of a symmetric session key.

sections.heading: Hash functions, digital signatures and certificates
sections.body:
A **cryptographic hash function** maps any message to a fixed-size **message digest**. Properties: one-way (pre-image resistant), second pre-image resistant and **collision resistant**; a one-bit change alters the digest completely. **MD5** gives 128 bits (broken), **SHA-1** 160 bits (deprecated), **SHA-256** 256 bits (SHA-2 family); SHA-3 is the newest standard. Passwords should be stored as **salted hashes**. A **MAC/HMAC** is a hash computed with a secret key.
**Digital signature**: the sender hashes the message and encrypts the digest with **her private key**; the receiver decrypts it with the sender's **public key** and compares with a fresh hash. It gives **authentication, integrity and non-repudiation** (not confidentiality by itself).
A **digital certificate** (X.509 format) binds a public key to an identity. It contains the subject's name and **public key**, serial number, validity period, the **issuing Certifying Authority's (CA) name** and the CA's own digital signature. Certificates are based on public-key cryptography and come in various key strengths.
**PKI** (Public Key Infrastructure) = CAs, Registration Authorities, certificate repositories and **Certificate Revocation Lists (CRL)**. In India, CAs are licensed by the **Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA)** under the IT Act.

sections.heading: Firewalls, IDS/IPS and VPN
sections.body:
A **firewall** is hardware or software that monitors and filters traffic between a trusted internal network and an untrusted network (the Internet) according to security rules. It can be network-based or host-based (personal firewall).
- **DMZ (demilitarised zone)**: a separate network segment for public servers (web, mail), placed between two firewalls or on a third firewall interface.
- **Proxy server**: makes requests on behalf of clients, hiding internal addresses and caching content.
- **IDS** (Intrusion Detection System) monitors and **alerts**; **IPS** (Intrusion Prevention System) also **blocks**. Detection is **signature-based** (known patterns) or **anomaly-based** (deviation from normal behaviour); NIDS watches the network, HIDS a host.
- **Honeypot**: a decoy system to attract and study attackers.
- **VPN** (Virtual Private Network): an encrypted **tunnel** over a public network (using IPSec or SSL/TLS) so remote users or branch offices connect securely.

sections.heading: Authentication and access control
sections.body:
**Authentication** verifies **who** you are; **authorisation** decides **what** you may do; **accounting** records what you did (together AAA). Identification (claiming an identity, e.g. a user name) comes first.
**Authentication factors:**
- **Something you know**: password, PIN, security question.
- **Something you have**: OTP token, smart card, mobile phone.
- **Something you are**: **biometrics** — fingerprint, iris, retina, face, voice; behavioural biometrics such as signature or typing rhythm.
Using two different factors is **two-factor authentication (2FA)**; more is **MFA**. Biometric accuracy is judged by **FAR** (false acceptance rate) and **FRR** (false rejection rate).
**CAPTCHA** (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) blocks bots. **Kerberos** is a ticket-based network authentication protocol using a trusted **Key Distribution Center** (Authentication Server + Ticket Granting Server) and symmetric keys. **Single sign-on (SSO)** lets one login access many systems.
**Access control models**: **DAC** (discretionary — the owner grants rights, e.g. file permissions), **MAC** (mandatory — system-enforced labels and clearances, e.g. military) and **RBAC** (role-based — rights attached to job roles). The **principle of least privilege** gives each user only the access needed.
**Strong passwords**: long, mixed character classes, not reused; change defaults.

sections.heading: Secure protocols: SSL/TLS, HTTPS, IPSec, SSH
sections.body:
- **SSL/TLS** (Secure Sockets Layer, developed by Netscape; its successor is Transport Layer Security) secures data **between the application layer and the transport layer** — it runs on top of TCP, uses a dedicated TCP connection, and requires a **server certificate**. The handshake authenticates the server, agrees on algorithms and exchanges a session key (public-key), after which data is encrypted symmetrically. It does **not** operate between the network and transport layers.
- **HTTPS** = HTTP over TLS, default **port 443**; browsers show a padlock.
- **IPSec** secures traffic at the **network layer**: **AH** (Authentication Header — integrity and authentication) and **ESP** (Encapsulating Security Payload — adds encryption); **transport mode** protects the payload, **tunnel mode** the whole packet (used in VPNs).
- **SSH** (port 22): encrypted remote login and file transfer (SCP/SFTP), replacing Telnet and rlogin.
- **E-mail security**: **PGP** (Pretty Good Privacy, Phil Zimmermann) and **S/MIME**.
- **Wi-Fi security**: WEP is broken; use **WPA2/WPA3**.

sections.heading: Information Technology Act, 2000: overview
sections.body:
The **Information Technology Act, 2000** (Act No. 21 of 2000) is India's primary law on e-commerce and cyber crime. It came into force on **17 October 2000** and is based on the **UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce (1996)**. As originally enacted it had **94 sections in 13 chapters and 4 schedules**.
**Main objectives**: legal recognition of **electronic records** (Section 4) and **electronic signatures** (Section 5); e-governance; regulation of **Certifying Authorities** by the **Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA)** (Section 17); defining cyber contraventions and offences.
**Section 3** authenticates electronic records by a digital signature using an **asymmetric crypto system and hash function**.
The **IT (Amendment) Act, 2008** (in force from 27 October 2009) made signatures technology-neutral ('electronic signature'), added Sections 66A–66F, 67A, 67B, 69A, 69B and 72A, and made **CERT-In** the national agency for incident response (**Section 70B**); **Section 70A** provides for a national nodal agency for critical information infrastructure (NCIIPC).
**Not applicable** (First Schedule) to: negotiable instruments other than cheques, powers of attorney, trusts, wills, and contracts for sale or conveyance of immovable property.
**Section 75**: the Act also applies to offences committed **outside India** if they involve a computer system located in India. **Section 78**: offences are investigated by a police officer **not below the rank of Inspector**. **Section 79** protects intermediaries that observe due diligence (safe harbour). The Cyber Appellate Tribunal (Section 48) was merged into **TDSAT** in 2017.

sections.heading: IT Act: important offences and penalties
sections.body:
Civil contraventions (**Section 43**) lead to **compensation** to the affected person, decided by an adjudicating officer; criminal offences (Sections 65–74) lead to **imprisonment and/or fine**. Remember the pattern by section number (see table). Notes:
- **Section 66A** (sending offensive messages) was **struck down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)** as violating freedom of speech; it is no longer law.
- **Section 66F (cyber terrorism)** carries the heaviest punishment: imprisonment that may extend to **life**.
- **Section 69** lets the government intercept, monitor or decrypt information; **Section 69A** lets it **block public access** to websites/content in the interest of sovereignty, security, public order etc.

sections.heading: Related laws, IPR, agencies and cyber ethics
sections.body:
- **New criminal laws**: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the IPC and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 replaced the Indian Evidence Act (electronic records remain admissible as evidence).
- **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023**: governs processing of digital personal data (Data Principal, Data Fiduciary, Data Protection Board). Check a current source for which provisions are in force.
- **Agencies**: **CERT-In** (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, under MeitY) handles cyber-security incidents; **NCIIPC** protects critical information infrastructure; the **National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal** and helpline **1930** (run under the Ministry of Home Affairs' I4C) take citizen complaints.
- **Intellectual Property Rights (IPR)** are granted for a **limited period**: **copyright** (software is protected as a literary work under the Copyright Act, 1957; generally the author's life + 60 years), **patent** (20 years under the Patents Act, 1970), **trademark** (10 years, renewable), plus designs and geographical indications. **Software piracy** and **plagiarism** violate IPR.
- **Cyber ethics / netiquette**: respect privacy, avoid piracy and plagiarism, credit sources, manage your **digital footprint**.

workedExamples.problem: Encrypt 'DSSSB EXAM' with a Caesar cipher of key 3, then show how many keys an attacker must try in the worst case.
workedExamples.solution:
Shift each letter 3 places forward (wrap Z → C):
D→G, S→V, S→V, S→V, B→E, E→H, X→A (X=23, 23 + 3 = 26 → 0 = A), A→D, M→P.
Ciphertext = **GVVVE HADP**.
Decryption shifts back by 3. Only 25 non-trivial shifts exist, so a brute-force attacker needs at most **25** trials — Caesar is insecure.

workedExamples.problem: Encrypt 'COMPUTER' with a rail-fence (depth 2) transposition cipher.
workedExamples.solution:
Write letters alternately on two rails:
- Rail 1 (positions 1, 3, 5, 7): C, M, U, E
- Rail 2 (positions 2, 4, 6, 8): O, P, T, R
Read rail 1 then rail 2: **CMUEOPTR**.
The letters are unchanged, only rearranged — that is what makes it a transposition cipher.

workedExamples.problem: RSA with p = 5, q = 11 and e = 3. Find n, φ(n), d, encrypt M = 9 and check the decryption.
Diffie–Hellman with p = 23, g = 5. Alice's secret a = 4, Bob's secret b = 3. Find the public values and the shared key.
workedExamples.solution:
Alice: A = 5⁴ mod 23 = 625 mod 23; 23 × 27 = 621 → **A = 4**.
Bob: B = 5³ mod 23 = 125 mod 23; 23 × 5 = 115 → **B = 10**.
Alice computes K = Bᵃ = 10⁴ mod 23 = 10000 mod 23; 23 × 434 = 9982 → **18**.
Bob computes K = Aᵇ = 4³ mod 23 = 64 mod 23 = **18**.
Both get the shared key **18** without ever sending it.

workedExamples.problem: (a) A company of 10 employees wants every pair to talk privately. How many keys are needed with symmetric and with asymmetric cryptography? (b) How many keys must be tried, in the worst case and on average, to brute-force DES? (c) How many 4-letter passwords using only lowercase letters exist?
workedExamples.solution:
(a) Symmetric: n(n − 1)/2 = 10 × 9 / 2 = **45** secret keys. Asymmetric: 10 key pairs = **20** keys.
(b) DES key = 56 bits → worst case 2⁵⁶ ≈ 7.2 × 10¹⁶ keys; on average half, 2⁵⁵ ≈ 3.6 × 10¹⁶.
(c) 26⁴ = **456,976** passwords — far too few, which is why long passwords with mixed character sets are recommended.

workedExamples.problem: Identify the IT Act section for each case: (i) a person uses a colleague's net-banking password to transfer money; (ii) a fraudster on a call pretends to be a bank officer and collects OTPs through a fake website; (iii) an employee alters the source code of the company's billing software to hide errors; (iv) someone publishes private photographs of a person without consent; (v) a group attacks the power-grid control systems to threaten national security.
workedExamples.solution:
(i) Fraudulent use of another person's password → **Section 66C** (identity theft): up to 3 years and fine up to ₹1 lakh (with Section 66 for the computer-related offence).
(ii) Cheating by personation using a computer resource → **Section 66D**: up to 3 years and fine up to ₹1 lakh.
(iii) Tampering with computer source documents → **Section 65**: up to 3 years, or fine up to ₹2 lakh, or both.
(iv) Violation of privacy → **Section 66E**: up to 3 years, or fine up to ₹2 lakh, or both.
(v) Cyber terrorism → **Section 66F**: imprisonment that may extend to life.

pitfalls: A worm spreads by itself over networks; a virus needs a host file and user action; a Trojan does not replicate at all.
Digital signatures use the sender's private key to sign and the sender's public key to verify; confidentiality uses the receiver's public key.
A digital signature gives authentication, integrity and non-repudiation, not confidentiality.
A digital certificate does include the issuing CA's name and is signed by the CA; certificates are not limited to one key strength.
SSL/TLS works between the transport and application layers (over TCP), not between the network and transport layers; IPSec is the network-layer protocol.
DES has a 64-bit block but only a 56-bit effective key; AES has a 128-bit block for all key sizes.
Hashing is one-way; it is not encryption and cannot be 'decrypted'.
Passive attacks (eavesdropping, traffic analysis) are prevented; active attacks (masquerade, replay, modification, DoS) are detected and recovered from.
Section 66A of the IT Act was struck down in 2015; do not quote it as current law.
The IT Act came into force on 17 October 2000; the amendment was passed in 2008 and took effect in 2009.
An IDS only alerts; an IPS can block traffic.
Authentication (who you are) is different from authorisation (what you may access).
quickRevision: Worm = self-replicating over network; Trojan = disguised, non-replicating; ransomware = encrypts and demands payment.
DES: 64-bit block, 56-bit key, 16 rounds. AES: 128-bit block, 128/192/256-bit keys, 10/12/14 rounds.
RSA security rests on factoring; Diffie–Hellman on the discrete logarithm problem.
Symmetric keys for n users: n(n − 1)/2; asymmetric: 2n.
Packet-filter firewall checks IP addresses and ports; application gateway (proxy) inspects content.
Authentication factors: something you know, have, are.
HTTPS uses TLS on port 443; SSH uses port 22; IPSec has AH and ESP.
IT Act 2000 is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law; 94 sections, 13 chapters, 4 schedules originally.
Sec 65 tampering source code; 66 hacking; 66C identity theft; 66D personation; 66E privacy; 66F cyber terrorism; 67 obscenity.
CERT-In is the national incident-response agency (Sec 70B); CCA licenses Certifying Authorities.
Cyber crime helpline 1930; patents last 20 years, copyright generally life + 60 years in India.
